citation.title: Sharp bounds on the variance in randomized experiments

standing_assumptions: [Population and design: Section 2, p. 851 (PDF p. 2)] Consider a population $U_N$ consisting of $N \ge 4$ units. From $U_N$, $n$ units are randomly sampled into the experimental sample, and the remaining $N - n$ units are left unsampled. Of the $n$ sampled units, $m \ge 2$ units are randomly assigned to the treatment condition, and $n - m \ge 2$ units are randomly assigned to the control condition. Let the indicator variable $X_i^T$ be one if unit $i$ is assigned to the treatment condition, and let the indicator $X_i^C$ be one if unit $i$ is assigned to the control condition. If $X_i^T = X_i^C = 0$, then the unit is unsampled. Since units are sampled without replacement, $X_i^T + X_i^C \le 1$. Without loss of generality, assume an index ordering $i = 1, \ldots, N$ such that those assigned to treatment come first, $X_1^T, \ldots, X_m^T = 1$, and those assigned to control come after, $X_{m+1}^C, \ldots, X_n^C = 1$, and the remaining $N - n$ unsampled units, if any, come last. Associated with each unit $i$ are two potential outcomes [13, 15] under control and treatment, respectively: $y_{0i}$ and $y_{1i}$. For each unit $i$, the analyst then observes $y_{0i}$ when $X_i^C = 1$ and $y_{1i}$ when $X_i^T = 1$. Given elements $v_i, w_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, N$, we define the finite population mean $\mu_N(v)$, finite population variance $\sigma_N^2(v)$ and finite population covariance $\sigma_N(v, w)$, respectively, as $\mu_N(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N v_i$, $\sigma_N^2(v) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\{v_i - \mu_N(v)\}^2$, $\sigma_N(v, w) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\{v_i - \mu_N(v)\}\{w_i - \mu_N(w)\}$. The average treatment effect for the population $U_N$ is $\tau_N = \mu_N(y_1) - \mu_N(y_0)$. The difference-in-means estimator of $\tau_N$ is (1) $\hat\tau_N = \hat\mu_N(y_1) - \hat\mu_N(y_0) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m y_{1i} - \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=m+1}^n y_{0i}$, with $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat\tau_N) = \tau_N$, where the expectation operator $\mathrm{E}_X$ averages over all $\binom{N}{n}\binom{n}{m}$ possible treatment assignments. Our inferential target is the variance of $\hat\tau_N$. Adapting Freedman [3], Proposition 1, the variance is (2) $V_N = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [Reading: the potential outcomes are deterministic (p. 850: 'a nonparametric model of deterministic potential outcomes'); the only randomness is the assignment, the $\binom{N}{n}\binom{n}{m}$ assignments being equally likely; $\mathrm{E}_X$, $\mathrm{Var}_X$ and $\mathrm{P}$ refer to it.] [Marginal variance estimators: p. 852 (PDF p. 3)] By Cochran [1], Theorem 2.4, unbiased estimators of $\sigma_N^2(y_1)$ and $\sigma_N^2(y_0)$ are $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) = \frac{N-1}{N(m-1)}\sum_{i=1}^m\{y_{1i} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\}^2$, $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) = \frac{N-1}{N(n-m-1)}\sum_{i=m+1}^n\{y_{0i} - \hat\mu_N(y_0)\}^2$. [The case $n = N$: Section 2.1, pp. 852–853 (PDF pp. 3–4)] When $n = N$, the sampling variance of the difference-in-means estimator reduces to (3) $V_n = \frac{1}{n-1}\left\{\frac{n-m}{m}\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \frac{m}{n-m}\sigma_n^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_n(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. (4) $\hat V_n^a = \frac{n}{n-1}\left\{\frac{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1)}{m} + \frac{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)}{n-m}\right\}$. (5) $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat V_n^a - V_n) = (n-1)^{-1}\{\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \sigma_n^2(y_0) - 2\sigma_n(y_1, y_0)\} \ge 0$. (6) $\hat V_n^{b\pm} = \frac{1}{n-1}\left[\frac{n-m}{m}\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \frac{m}{n-m}\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0) \pm 2\{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1)\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)\}^{1/2}\right]$. [Marginal distributions and sharp bounds: Section 3, p. 853 (PDF p. 4)] Let $G_N(y) = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I(y_{1i} \le y)$ and $F_N(y) = N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I(y_{0i} \le y)$ be the marginal distribution functions of $y_1$ and $y_0$, respectively. Define their left-continuous inverses as $G_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : G_N(y) \ge u\}$ and $F_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : F_N(y) \ge u\}$. Define also (7) $\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(u)\,du - \mu_N(y_1)\mu_N(y_0)$, $\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(1-u)\,du - \mu_N(y_1)\mu_N(y_0)$. [p. 853] $V_N^H = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)\right\}$, $V_N^L = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [Estimators: p. 854 (PDF p. 5)] In practice, we observe neither $G_N$ nor $F_N$, but rather their estimates $\hat G_N(y) = m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^T I(y_{1i} \le y)$, $\hat F_N(y) = (n-m)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^C I(y_{0i} \le y)$ and left-continuous inverses $\hat G_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : \hat G_N(y) \ge u\} = y_{1(\lceil mu\rceil)}$, $\hat F_N^{-1}(u) = \inf\{y : \hat F_N(y) \ge u\} = y_{0(m+\lceil (n-m)u\rceil)}$, where $y_{1(1)} \le \cdots \le y_{1(m)}$ and $y_{0(m+1)} \le \cdots \le y_{0(n)}$ are the ordered observed outcomes, and $\lceil x\rceil$ denotes the smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$. Substituting $(\hat G_N, \hat F_N)$ for $(G_N, F_N)$ in (7) yields an interval estimator $[\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0), \hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)]$ for $\sigma_N(y_1, y_0)$: $\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 \hat G_N^{-1}(u)\hat F_N^{-1}(u)\,du - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$, $\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \int_0^1 \hat G_N^{-1}(u)\hat F_N^{-1}(1-u)\,du - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$. Let the $[0, 1]$-partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n} = \{p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_P\}$ be the ordered distinct elements of $\{0, 1/m, 2/m, \ldots, 1\} \cup \{0, 1/(n-m), 2/(n-m), \ldots, 1\}$. Let $y_{1[i]} = y_{1(\lceil mp_i\rceil)}$ and $y_{0[i]} = y_{0\{m+\lceil (n-m)p_i\rceil\}}$. The inverses $\hat G_N^{-1}$ and $\hat F_N^{-1}$ are piecewise constant since $\hat G_N^{-1}(u) = y_{1[i]}$ and $\hat F_N^{-1}(u) = y_{0[i]}$ for $u \in (p_{i-1}, p_i]$. In addition, the symmetry $p_i = 1 - p_{P-i}$ implies that $p_i - p_{i-1} = p_{P+1-i} - p_{P-i}$. Thus, $[\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0), \hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)]$ reduces to (8) $\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \sum_{i=1}^P (p_i - p_{i-1})y_{1[i]}y_{0[i]} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$, $\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \sum_{i=1}^P (p_i - p_{i-1})y_{1[i]}y_{0[P+1-i]} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\hat\mu_N(y_0)$, where $\hat\mu_N(y_1)$ and $\hat\mu_N(y_0)$ are as defined in (1). Substituting $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1)$, $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0)$, and (8) for $\{\sigma_N^2(y_1), \sigma_N^2(y_0), \sigma_N(y_1, y_0)\}$ in the expressions for $V_N^L$ and $V_N^H$, we obtain the interval estimator $[\hat V_N^L, \hat V_N^H]$ for $V_N$: (9) $\hat V_N^H = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)\right\}$, $\hat V_N^L = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [Asymptotic setting: Section 4, p. 855 (PDF p. 6)] Let $\{U_N\}_N$ be a nested sequence of finite populations. The potential outcomes $y_1$ and $y_0$ of each unit are fixed, and hence the population grows deterministically. As in Isaki and Fuller [10], we do not assume that the sequences of treatment assignments are nested; instead, each $U_N$ hosts its own random assignment. Let $H_N(\cdot, \cdot)$ be the joint distribution function of $(y_1, y_0)$ for $U_N$. [Conditions of Proposition 1, p. 855 (PDF p. 6), 'as $N \to \infty$'] 1. $(m/N, n/N) \to (\theta\rho, \theta)$ for $\theta \in (0, 1]$ and $\rho \in (0, 1)$; 2. $H_N$ converges weakly to a limit distribution $H$ with marginals $G(y) = H(y, \infty)$ and $F(y) = H(\infty, y)$; 3. $G_N(y) \to G(y)$ at any discontinuity point of $G$, and $F_N(y) \to F(y)$ at any discontinuity point of $F$; 4. The sequences of distributions represented by $\{G_N\}_N$ and $\{F_N\}_N$ are uniformly square-integrable. That is, as $\beta \to \infty$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i : y_{1i}^2 \ge \beta} y_{1i}^2\right\}$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i : y_{0i}^2 \ge \beta} y_{0i}^2\right\} \to 0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 1 (Hoeffding) and the sentence 'Lemma 1 implies that $[V_N^L, V_N^H]$ is the sharpest interval bound for $V_N$'; with equation (2)
canonical_claim.location: p. 853 (PDF p. 4); equation (2) on p. 851 (PDF p. 2); proof of Lemma 1 on pp. 859–860 (PDF pp. 10–11)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 851 (PDF p. 2)] The difference-in-means estimator of $\tau_N$ is (1) $\hat\tau_N = \hat\mu_N(y_1) - \hat\mu_N(y_0) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m y_{1i} - \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=m+1}^n y_{0i}$, with $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat\tau_N) = \tau_N$, where the expectation operator $\mathrm{E}_X$ averages over all $\binom{N}{n}\binom{n}{m}$ possible treatment assignments. Our inferential target is the variance of $\hat\tau_N$. Adapting Freedman [3], Proposition 1, the variance is (2) $V_N = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N(y_1, y_0)\right\}$. [p. 853 (PDF p. 4)] LEMMA 1 (Hoeffding). Given only $G_N$ and $F_N$ and no other information on the joint distribution of $(y_1, y_0)$, the bound $\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) \le \sigma_N(y_1, y_0) \le \sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)$ is sharp. The upper bound is attained if $y_1$ and $y_0$ are comonotonic, that is, $(y_1, y_0) \sim \{G_N^{-1}(U), F_N^{-1}(U)\}$ for a uniform random variable $U$ on $[0, 1]$. The lower bound is attained if $y_1$ and $y_0$ are countermonotonic, that is, $(y_1, y_0) \sim \{G_N^{-1}(U), F_N^{-1}(1 - U)\}$. [p. 853] Lemma 1 implies that $[V_N^L, V_N^H]$ is the sharpest interval bound for $V_N$: $V_N^H = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)\right\}$, $V_N^L = \frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N-m}{m}\sigma_N^2(y_1) + \frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m}\sigma_N^2(y_0) + 2\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0)\right\}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The population, the design, $\mu_N$, $\sigma_N^2$, $\sigma_N(\cdot,\cdot)$, $\tau_N$, $\hat\tau_N$, $\mathrm{E}_X$, $V_N$ of (2), $\hat\sigma_N^2$, $G_N$, $F_N$ and their left-continuous inverses, (7), $V_N^H$, $V_N^L$, $\hat G_N$, $\hat F_N$, the partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n}$, (8), (9), and for $n = N$ (3), (4), (6) are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. [Proof of Lemma 1, pp. 859–860 (PDF pp. 10–11)] Let $H_N(y_1, y_0)$ be the joint distribution function of $(y_1, y_0)$, and define two other distributions $H_N^H(y_1, y_0) = \min\{G_N(y_1), F_N(y_0)\}$ and $H_N^L(y_1, y_0) = \max\{0, G_N(y_1) + F_N(y_0) - 1\}$. All three distributions have the same marginals $G_N$ and $F_N$. Defining $\mathrm{E}_Q$ as the expectation operator with respect to a distribution $Q$, a result by Hoeffding, recounted in Tchen [17], shows that $\mathrm{E}_{H_N^L}(y_1y_0) \le \mathrm{E}_{H_N}(y_1y_0) \le \mathrm{E}_{H_N^H}(y_1y_0)$. Since $\{G_N^{-1}(U), F_N^{-1}(U)\} \sim H_N^H$ and $\{G_N^{-1}(U), F_N^{-1}(1-U)\} \sim H_N^L$, the lower and upper bounds are equivalent to $\mathrm{E}_{H_N^H}(y_1y_0) = \int_0^1G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(u)\,du$, $\mathrm{E}_{H_N^L}(y_1y_0) = \int_0^1G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(1-u)\,du$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Reading for a finite population: the populations of $N$ units with marginals $G_N$ and $F_N$ are those with outcome pairs $(y_{1i}, y_{0\pi(i)})$, $\pi$ a permutation of $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. Write $y_{1(1)} \le \cdots \le y_{1(N)}$ and $y_{0(1)} \le \cdots \le y_{0(N)}$ for the ordered potential outcomes of the population. (i) $\int_0^1G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(u)\,du = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ny_{1(i)}y_{0(i)}$ and $\int_0^1G_N^{-1}(u)F_N^{-1}(1-u)\,du = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ny_{1(i)}y_{0(N+1-i)}$. (ii) [Rearrangement inequality] For every permutation $\pi$, $\frac1N\sum_iy_{1(i)}y_{0(N+1-i)} \le \frac1N\sum_iy_{1i}y_{0\pi(i)} \le \frac1N\sum_iy_{1(i)}y_{0(i)}$; the right-hand bound is attained by the pairing that matches the ordered values (comonotonic), the left-hand bound by the pairing that matches them in opposite order (countermonotonic). (iii) $\mu_N$ and $\sigma_N^2$ of each margin do not depend on $\pi$, and $V_N$ of (2) is increasing in $\sigma_N(y_1, y_0)$ with coefficient $2/(N-1) > 0$; hence $V_N^L \le V_N \le V_N^H$ for every pairing, and both ends are attained. (iv) [Equation (2)] Over the $\binom{N}{n}\binom{n}{m}$ equally likely assignments, $\mathrm{E}_X(\hat\tau_N) = \tau_N$ and $\mathrm{Var}_X(\hat\tau_N) = V_N$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P022-H2; both readers report that it held up (the proof followed, and all pairings enumerated for small populations; equation (2) re-derived and confirmed by exact enumeration with $n = N$ and $n < N$). The lemma is printed for joint distributions with the given marginals. For a population of $N$ units the joint distributions that can occur are the pairings, and the comonotonic and countermonotonic distributions are themselves pairings, which is what makes the interval $[V_N^L, V_N^H]$ the smallest one containing every value of $V_N$ compatible with $G_N$ and $F_N$. Equation (2), which the paper adapts from Freedman (2008), is part of this target because the claim is about the variance of $\hat\tau_N$; (3) is its case $n = N$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, sentence after equation (9): $\hat V_N^H$ is never greater than $\hat V_N^{b+}$, and $\hat V_N^L$ is never smaller than $\hat V_N^{b-}$
canonical_claim.location: p. 854 (PDF p. 5); (4) and (6) on pp. 852–853 (PDF pp. 3–4); Introduction, p. 850 (PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 850 (PDF p. 1)] The upper bound is never larger than and often smaller than conventional approximations. [p. 852 (PDF p. 3)] Neyman [13] proposed an estimator of $V_n$ that uses the inequality $2\sigma_n(y_1, y_0) \le 2\{\sigma_n^2(y_1)\sigma_n^2(y_0)\}^{1/2} \le \sigma_n^2(y_1) + \sigma_n^2(y_0)$, by application of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means. [p. 854 (PDF p. 5)] Since Lemma 1 applies to the sample populations as well, it follows that $\hat V_N^H$ is never greater than $\hat V_N^{b+}$, and $\hat V_N^L$ is never smaller than $\hat V_N^{b-}$. [Formal reading, for $n = N$, the case in which (4) and (6) are defined] For every assignment, $\hat V_n^{b-} \le \hat V_n^L \le \hat V_n^H \le \hat V_n^{b+} \le \hat V_n^a$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The population, the design, $\mu_N$, $\sigma_N^2$, $\sigma_N(\cdot,\cdot)$, $\tau_N$, $\hat\tau_N$, $\mathrm{E}_X$, $V_N$ of (2), $\hat\sigma_N^2$, $G_N$, $F_N$ and their left-continuous inverses, (7), $V_N^H$, $V_N^L$, $\hat G_N$, $\hat F_N$, the partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n}$, (8), (9), and for $n = N$ (3), (4), (6) are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. $\hat V_n^a$ is (4) and $\hat V_n^{b\pm}$ is (6), both defined in Section 2.1 for $n = N$; $\hat V_N^H$, $\hat V_N^L$ are (9) with (8).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (i) Let $\tilde\sigma_1^2 = \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\{y_{1i} - \hat\mu_N(y_1)\}^2$ and $\tilde\sigma_0^2 = \frac{1}{n-m}\sum_{i=m+1}^n\{y_{0i} - \hat\mu_N(y_0)\}^2$ be the variances of the two empirical distributions. Then $\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) \le \hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)$ and $|\hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0)|, |\hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0)| \le \{\tilde\sigma_1^2\tilde\sigma_0^2\}^{1/2}$ (Lemma 1 for the empirical distributions, or the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the centred quantile functions $\hat G_N^{-1}$, $\hat F_N^{-1}$ on $[0, 1]$). (ii) $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1) = \frac{(N-1)m}{N(m-1)}\tilde\sigma_1^2 \ge \tilde\sigma_1^2$ and $\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0) = \frac{(N-1)(n-m)}{N(n-m-1)}\tilde\sigma_0^2 \ge \tilde\sigma_0^2$, because $N \ge m$ and $N \ge n - m$. (iii) Hence $-\{\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1)\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0)\}^{1/2} \le \hat\sigma_N^L(y_1, y_0) \le \hat\sigma_N^H(y_1, y_0) \le \{\hat\sigma_N^2(y_1)\hat\sigma_N^2(y_0)\}^{1/2}$; with $n = N$ the coefficients of (9) and (6) coincide ($\frac{N-m}{m} = \frac{n-m}{m}$ and $\frac{N-(n-m)}{n-m} = \frac{m}{n-m}$), which gives $\hat V_n^{b-} \le \hat V_n^L \le \hat V_n^H \le \hat V_n^{b+}$. (iv) $2\{\hat\sigma_n^2(y_1)\hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)\}^{1/2} \le \hat\sigma_n^2(y_1) + \hat\sigma_n^2(y_0)$, $\frac{n-m}{m} + 1 = \frac nm$ and $\frac{m}{n-m} + 1 = \frac{n}{n-m}$ give $\hat V_n^{b+} \le \hat V_n^a$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P022-H3; both readers report that it held up (proved, and confirmed by exact enumeration). The paper writes $\hat V_N^{b+}$ and $\hat V_N^{b-}$ with subscript $N$ although (6) defines $\hat V_n^{b\pm}$ only for $n = N$; the target is that case. The paper's one-line justification ('Lemma 1 applies to the sample populations as well') leaves out step (ii), that the unbiased variance estimators are at least the variances of the empirical distributions. 'often smaller' is not a mathematical statement and is not part of the target. For $n < N$ the readers also verified $\hat V_N^H \le s_1^2/m + s_0^2/(n-m)$, which is not printed and is not part of the target.

canonical_claim.location: p. 855 (PDF p. 6); proof on pp. 862–863 (PDF pp. 13–14)
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 1. Suppose the following conditions hold as $N \to \infty$: 1. $(m/N, n/N) \to (\theta\rho, \theta)$ for $\theta \in (0, 1]$ and $\rho \in (0, 1)$; 2. $H_N$ converges weakly to a limit distribution $H$ with marginals $G(y) = H(y, \infty)$ and $F(y) = H(\infty, y)$; 3. $G_N(y) \to G(y)$ at any discontinuity point of $G$, and $F_N(y) \to F(y)$ at any discontinuity point of $F$; 4. The sequences of distributions represented by $\{G_N\}_N$ and $\{F_N\}_N$ are uniformly square-integrable. That is, as $\beta \to \infty$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac1N\sum_{i : y_{1i}^2 \ge \beta}y_{1i}^2\right\}$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac1N\sum_{i : y_{0i}^2 \ge \beta}y_{0i}^2\right\} \to 0$. Then for the collection $\mathcal{H}$ of all bivariate distributions with marginals $G$ and $F$, the moments of each $h \in \mathcal{H}$ exist up to second order and $NV_N^H \to \frac{1-\theta\rho}{\theta\rho}\mathrm{Var}_H(y_1) + \frac{1-\theta(1-\rho)}{\theta(1-\rho)}\mathrm{Var}_H(y_0) + 2\sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\mathrm{Cov}_h(y_1, y_0)$, $NV_N^L \to \frac{1-\theta\rho}{\theta\rho}\mathrm{Var}_H(y_1) + \frac{1-\theta(1-\rho)}{\theta(1-\rho)}\mathrm{Var}_H(y_0) + 2\inf_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\mathrm{Cov}_h(y_1, y_0)$. Moreover, $(\hat V_N^H - V_N^H, \hat V_N^L - V_N^L) = o_P(1/N)$.

[Section 4, p. 855 (PDF p. 6)] Let $\{U_N\}_N$ be a nested sequence of finite populations. The potential outcomes $y_1$ and $y_0$ of each unit are fixed, and hence the population grows deterministically. […] each $U_N$ hosts its own random assignment. Let $H_N(\cdot, \cdot)$ be the joint distribution function of $(y_1, y_0)$ for $U_N$. $\mathrm{Var}_H$ and $\mathrm{Cov}_h$ are the variance and covariance under the distributions $H$ and $h$. $o_P(1/N)$: $N(\hat V_N^H - V_N^H) \to 0$ and $N(\hat V_N^L - V_N^L) \to 0$ in probability, the probability being that of the random assignment for $U_N$. [Proof, stage (iv), p. 863 (PDF p. 14)] Define the distributions $H^H(y_1, y_0) = \min\{G(y_1), F(y_0)\}$ and $H^L(y_1, y_0) = \max\{0, G(y_1) + F(y_0) - 1\}$, both of which have marginals $G$ and $F$. Using Hoeffding's result from the proof of Lemma 1, we have that $\mathrm{E}_{H^H}(y_1y_0) = \sup_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\mathrm{E}_h(y_1y_0)$, $\mathrm{E}_{H^L}(y_1y_0) = \inf_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\mathrm{E}_h(y_1y_0)$.

canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P022-H1. The proposition is touched by P022-E001 through its proof: the outline on p. 856 and stages (i)–(ii) on p. 862 pass through Lemma 2, which is false under conditions 1–3 (P022-T1). canonical_claim.location: p. 863 (PDF p. 14); Remark 3 on p. 856 (PDF p. 7); proof on pp. 863–869 (PDF pp. 14–20)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 863 (PDF p. 14)] PROPOSITION 2. Suppose conditions 1–3 of Proposition 1 hold, and that $y_1$ and $y_0$ are bounded: $|y_{1i}|, |y_{0i}| \le C < \infty$ for all $i$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, for any $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \varepsilon_3 > 0$ such that $\sum_i\varepsilon_i = \varepsilon$, $\mathrm{P}\left(N|\hat V_N^H - V_N^H| \ge \varepsilon\right) \le \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{C^4}{N}\kappa_1(\varepsilon_1)\right)$, $\mathrm{P}\left(N|\hat V_N^L - V_N^L| \ge \varepsilon\right) \le \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{C^4}{N}\left\{1/\varepsilon_1^2 + \kappa_2(\varepsilon_2) + \kappa_3(\varepsilon_3)\right\}\right)$, where $\kappa_1(\varepsilon_1)$, $\kappa_2(\varepsilon_2)$ and $\kappa_3(\varepsilon_3)$ depend on the limiting distribution $H$. [Remark 3, p. 856 (PDF p. 7)] If condition 4 of Proposition 1 is strengthened to require that $y_1$ and $y_0$ be bounded, then higher order rates of convergence can be obtained, namely that $\mathrm{P}(N|\hat V_N^H - V_N^H| > \varepsilon)$ and $\mathrm{P}(N|\hat V_N^L - V_N^L| > \varepsilon)$ are both of order $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$. Interested readers are referred to Proposition 2 in the Appendix.

canonical_claim.location: p. 856 (PDF p. 7); Remark 4 on p. 857 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 856 (PDF p. 7)] The proof of the following corollary follows directly from Freedman [3], Theorem 1, and associated remarks. COROLLARY 1. Suppose that the support of $H$ is nonsingular and that conditions 1–3 of Proposition 1 hold. Suppose in addition that condition 4 is strengthened to require uniformly bounded third moments: $\sup_N\left\{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N|y_{1i}|^3\right\}$, $\sup_N\left\{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N|y_{0i}|^3\right\} < \infty$. Then $\frac{\hat\tau_N - \tau_N}{(\gamma\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}}$ converges weakly to the standard normal distribution where $\gamma = \lim_N(NV_N)/\lim_N(NV_N^H) \le 1$. [Remark 4, p. 857 (PDF p. 8)] As $\hat V_N^H$ is consistent for the sharp upper bound on $V_N$, then given large $N$, a confidence interval constructed as $\hat\tau_N \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}(\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}$ is asymptotically the narrowest Wald-type confidence interval assured to have at least the nominal coverage.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The population, the design, $\mu_N$, $\sigma_N^2$, $\sigma_N(\cdot,\cdot)$, $\tau_N$, $\hat\tau_N$, $\mathrm{E}_X$, $V_N$ of (2), $\hat\sigma_N^2$, $G_N$, $F_N$ and their left-continuous inverses, (7), $V_N^H$, $V_N^L$, $\hat G_N$, $\hat F_N$, the partition $\mathcal{P}_{m,n}$, (8), (9), and for $n = N$ (3), (4), (6) are transcribed in the standing assumptions, with locations. The nested sequence $\{U_N\}_N$, $H_N$, $H$, $G$, $F$, $\theta$, $\rho$ and conditions 1–4 of Proposition 1 are transcribed in the standing assumptions (Section 4, p. 855, PDF p. 6). Weak convergence is that of the distribution of the statistic under the random assignment for $U_N$, as $N \to \infty$. $\lim_N(NV_N^H)$ is the first limit of Proposition 1; $\lim_N(NV_N) = \frac{1-\theta\rho}{\theta\rho}\mathrm{Var}_H(y_1) + \frac{1-\theta(1-\rho)}{\theta(1-\rho)}\mathrm{Var}_H(y_0) + 2\mathrm{Cov}_H(y_1, y_0)$ (by (2) and conditions 1, 2 and 4). 'The support of $H$ is nonsingular' is read as: $H$ is not concentrated on a line (its covariance matrix is nonsingular). $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (i) For each $N$, $V_N \le V_N^H$ (Lemma 1, P022-T13), hence $\gamma \le 1$ when the limits exist and $\lim_N(NV_N^H) > 0$. (ii) $\frac1N\sum_{i : y_{1i}^2 \ge \beta}y_{1i}^2 \le \beta^{-1/2}\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N|y_{1i}|^3$ (and the same for $y_0$), so uniformly bounded third moments imply condition 4. (iii) For each $N$ and each assignment with $V_N > 0$ and $\hat V_N^H > 0$: $\frac{\hat\tau_N - \tau_N}{(\gamma\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}} = \frac{\hat\tau_N - \tau_N}{V_N^{1/2}}\left(\frac{NV_N}{\gamma N\hat V_N^H}\right)^{1/2}$. (iv) With $a = \frac{1-\theta\rho}{\theta\rho}$ and $b = \frac{1-\theta(1-\rho)}{\theta(1-\rho)}$: $ab = 1 + \frac{1-\theta}{\theta^2\rho(1-\rho)} \ge 1$, so $\lim_N(NV_N) \ge \mathrm{Var}_H\left(\sqrt a\,y_1 + y_0/\sqrt a\right)$, which is positive when $H$ is not concentrated on a line. (v) [Remark 4] If $Z_N = (\hat\tau_N - \tau_N)/(\gamma\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}$ converges weakly to the standard normal distribution, then $\mathrm{P}\left(|\hat\tau_N - \tau_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}(\hat V_N^H)^{1/2}\right) = \mathrm{P}\left(|Z_N| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}/\sqrt\gamma\right) \to 2\Phi\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}/\sqrt\gamma\right) - 1 \ge 1 - \alpha$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P022-H5. The central limit theorem for $(\hat\tau_N - \tau_N)/V_N^{1/2}$ is cited from Freedman (2008), Theorem 1 and associated remarks, and is not proved in the paper; a formalization would take it as a named axiom or as a hypothesis. P022-N002, which questioned whether the citation covers third moments and $n < N$, is rated not confirmed after the cited paper was read. The other input is the consistency of $N\hat V_N^H$ (Proposition 1, P022-T15), whose printed proof is touched by P022-E001 while its statement holds; the rating records P022-H5 as affected by P022-E001 for that reason. Remark 4 is an interpretive remark; its formal part is the coverage limit in (v). The words 'the narrowest … assured' (no variance input that is determined by the marginal distributions and lies below the sharp upper bound guarantees nominal coverage for every joint distribution compatible with them, because the bound is attained, and then $\gamma = 1$) are not a target.
